text.label: Demo report: fictional companies (Loopwell, Kinship, Amplo, Referrly, ShareMint) on .example domains; every number and page is made up
text.headline: Kinship sells the switch from Loopwell with a price on the page; Loopwell answers with [["Talk to sales"]]
text.lead: Loopwell leads on enterprise depth, fraud controls and review ratings, but it trails on {trail} of {crit} criteria, nearly all at the evaluation step: no public price, no self-serve setup, no migration help. Kinship has built a comparison page and a migration guide aimed at Loopwell's customers. The cheapest wins are pages and proof, not features.
text.matrixH: Loopwell trails on {trail} of {crit} criteria and leads outright on {lead}; the gaps cluster around pricing and switching
text.matrixP: Same criteria for every product. Each cell shows what was seen and a numbered source with the date it was checked. A red bar marks a criterion where Loopwell is behind the best competitor. Ratings count as ✓ at 4.5+ with 100+ reviews.
text.canvasH: Everyone crowds into the same curve on integrations; Loopwell's line drops exactly where buyers compare
text.canvasP: Blue Ocean strategy canvas: offering level 0–10 per factor, judged from the matrix rows named in each factor. Where lines run together, nobody wins; the gaps are where a move can differ.
text.errcH: Raise price clarity and switching help; create a proof library nobody else has
text.errcP: ERRC grid for Loopwell's next two quarters, drawn from the matrix and the canvas.
text.mapH: Loopwell sits alone in managed, referrals-only; Kinship and ShareMint sell suites from the self-serve side
text.mapP: Positions are judgments from the matrix rows on setup, pricing and breadth, not measured data.
text.winH: Loopwell wins on depth and trust, and loses before the first call
text.winP: Each point cites the sources behind it.
text.mxH: {qw} quick wins: mostly pages and proof that already exist inside the company
text.mxP: Each dot is a move from the table below. Black: optimize what exists; red outline: exploration bets.
text.opsP: ICE = impact × confidence × ease (each 1–10). "Observed" means the gap is visible on public pages; "hypothesis" means it still needs a test.
text.nextH: Three moves: show a price, answer the comparison page, help people switch in
text.nextP: Each has a hypothesis, a success metric and the cheapest way to test it.
text.planH: Full plan: all {n} moves, most valuable first
text.planP: For each move: the evidence, the competitor pages behind it, steps, metric, effort and risk. The top three also show alternatives, an experiment with a threshold and a pre-mortem.
text.dataH: Confidence {conf}%: public pages and review sites only
text.dataP: This teardown read vendor sites, review listings, a domain rank list, a funding database and web archive snapshots. It did not see traffic, win rates or loss reasons, so impact scores are estimates.
how: Checked sources: browser and web search available; traffic and CRM data not available. Asked 4 skippable questions; one was skipped.

Read each vendor's homepage, pricing, comparison and docs pages, review listings, a domain rank list, a funding database and archive snapshots from a year ago. Every cell records the page and the date.
Filled the same 17 criteria for all 5 products, marked one vendor's words about another as claims, and judged the canvas and the map from the matrix.
Scored moves with ICE, compared alternatives for the top 3, wrote experiments and pre-mortems, then validated the data and checked the page on desktop, tablet and phone.

1.h: If the pricing page shows a starting price, more qualified buyers will book a demo, because three of four rivals already answer the price question.
1.m: Demo requests from the pricing page per 1,000 visits
1.t: A/B on the pricing page for 4 weeks: starting price vs current

2.h: If buyers who read Kinship's page find a sourced answer from Loopwell, fewer will drop Loopwell from the shortlist.
2.m: Organic entries to the vs page and demo requests from it
2.t: Publish one page, link it from pricing, compare demos 6 weeks before and after

4.h: If case studies name the brand and one number, the homepage will earn more demo clicks, because buyers trust named proof more.
4.m: Homepage click rate on case studies and demo requests
4.t: Ask the two featured clients for permission; swap and compare 4 weeks

1.why: Loopwell's pricing page lists three revenue bands and asks for a call in each. Kinship, Referrly and ShareMint show prices; Kinship added an estimator this year.

evidence.t: Price from $399/month with an order-volume estimator
Estimator added in the last 12 months

steps: Pick one honest anchor: a starting price for the smallest band, or a range per band.
Add it to the pricing page with what is included and what changes the price.
Keep Talk to sales as the second action, not the only one.
Run the A/B for 4 weeks and compare qualified demos, not just clicks.
1.metric: Demo requests from the pricing page per 1,000 visits; share qualified by sales
1.risk: Anchoring too low; publish a starting price that sales already uses.
alt: Price estimator like Kinship's: stronger, but needs a pricing model sales agrees on; next step if the anchor works.
Gated price sheet behind email: rejected, buyers read it as hiding.
1.thr: Pricing-page demo rate +15% and qualified share not lower than control
1.pm: It failed because sales kept quoting differently from the page. Agree the anchor with sales before publishing.
copy: From $1,200 a month for brands up to $20m: anchors the smallest band.
Most clients pay $1,200–4,000 a month: a range lowers the fear of a high quote.

2.why: Kinship's comparison page targets Loopwell by name and is updated regularly. Loopwell has no comparison page, so buyers who search the two names find only Kinship's version.

evidence.t: Kinship vs Loopwell page, updated October 2026
Kinship's page says Loopwell has no Shopify app; the app store lists one
Loopwell app listed on AppShelf, 4.8 from 64 reviews

steps: List each claim on Kinship's page and check it against public sources; keep only what you can link.
Write a Loopwell vs Kinship page: where each fits, a sourced table and the date checked.
Link it from the pricing page and the footer.
Re-check the table every quarter and show the date.
2.metric: Organic entries to the page and demo requests from it
2.risk: Claims about a rival go stale; date every row and never state their price unless it is public.
alt: Reply in sales decks only: rejected, buyers search before they talk to sales.
Ask Kinship to correct the Shopify claim: worth doing as well, but does not answer the buyer.
2.thr: The page reaches the first results for the two names within 8 weeks and brings 5+ demos
2.pm: It failed because the page read as an attack. Lead with where each product fits, and keep the tone factual.

3.why: Kinship publishes a step-by-step guide for leaving Loopwell. Loopwell's docs have no guide for brands leaving other tools.

evidence.t: Migration guide aimed at Loopwell customers

steps: Write one migration guide per main rival: export, mapping, codes, go-live checklist.
Build an import for existing advocates and referral codes.
Offer a migration call in the guide.
3.metric: Deals that mention switching from a rival
3.risk: Promising a migration the team cannot staff; cap free migrations per month.

4.why: Both Loopwell case studies say a beauty brand and a fashion retailer. Kinship and Amplo name the brand and give one number each.

evidence.t: Six named brands with one result each
Named enterprise cases with ROI figures

steps: Ask the two featured clients for permission to name them.
Add the brand, one number and the period to each case.
Put the best number in the homepage hero.
4.metric: Homepage click rate on case studies; demo requests
4.risk: Clients say no; offer review rights and pick others with public results.
alt: Anonymous numbers in the hero: rejected, the gap is trust, not numbers.
Video testimonials: later, slower to produce.
4.pm: It failed because legal teams took 3 months. Start with clients who already spoke at events.

5.why: The homepage says weeks without a number. Kinship says 7 days and Referrly says 10 minutes.

evidence.t: Live in 7 days for Shopify stores

steps: Take the median go-live time of the last 10 launches.
State it on the homepage with what it includes.
Track it every month.
5.metric: Median days to go live; homepage demo rate
5.risk: Stating a number the team misses; use the median, not the best case.

6.why: Fraud control is the top theme in Loopwell's reviews and none of the four rivals publishes fraud numbers.

evidence.t: Fraud control among top review themes
Publishes research reports, none on fraud

steps: Aggregate blocked referrals across clients for 12 months, anonymized.
Publish a short report with method and limits.
Use it as the offer for visitors not ready for a demo.
6.metric: Report downloads and demos from them
6.risk: Client data: aggregate only, legal review before publishing.

7.why: Loopwell's demo form asks seven fields before any contact. Kinship starts a trial with an email address.

evidence.t: Trial starts with an email address

steps: Keep name, work email and company; move the rest to the call.
Add calendar booking after submit.
Compare completion and qualified share for 4 weeks.
7.metric: Form completion rate and qualified share
7.risk: More unqualified demos; qualify on the call.

8.why: Kinship, Amplo and ShareMint sell loyalty with referrals; Loopwell sells referrals only. Whether Loopwell's buyers want a suite is unknown.

evidence.t: Referral add-on moved into every paid plan

steps: Ask 8 clients what they use for loyalty and what they pay.
If 3+ would switch, build the smallest points feature with two clients.
Decide after 3 months.
8.metric: Clients willing to pilot; retention of pilot clients
8.risk: Splitting focus before the evaluation-stage gaps are fixed.

9.why: No analytics data was available for this teardown, so the effect of the page moves cannot be measured yet.

evidence.t: Kinship's estimator and vs page sit on the same path a buyer takes

steps: Tag pricing, comparison and demo pages as one funnel.
Report weekly: visits, demo requests, qualified demos.
Re-run this teardown with the data.
9.risk: Double-counted events; test in a staging property first.

sources.name: Web archive snapshots, Nov 2025 vs Nov 2026 (fictional)

ICE.d: Impact × Confidence × Ease, each 1–10. The bigger the product, the sooner to do it.

ERRC.d: The Blue Ocean grid: what to drop, cut, push above the industry and add that nobody offers.

Blue Ocean.d: Strategy of making the competition irrelevant by offering a different mix of value rather than more of the same.

strategy canvas.d: A line per product across the factors buyers compare. Where lines run together nobody wins; gaps show where to differ.

pre-mortem.d: Imagine the move failed in 3 months and explain why. The reasons become risks to close now.

A/B.d: Half the visitors see the new version, half the old one; the difference shows the effect.

MCP.d: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI assistants to use a product's data and actions.

API.d: A documented way for other software to read and change data in the product.

ROI.d: What a program earns compared with what it costs.

Shopify Plus.d: The plan larger Shopify stores use; a common size signal in ecommerce.
